title.title: Universal algebra and hardness results for constraint satisfaction problems

editorial_contributions.text:
Many natural decision problems like SAT or graph \(k\)-colourability can be expressed in terms of a decision problem of the following type CSP\((A)\): Let \(A\) be a finite relational structure of finite type and let \(I\) be a given structure of the same type. Does there exist a homomorphism from \(I\) to \(A\)? To each relational structure \(A\) naturally an algebra \({\mathbf A}\) is associated whose structure determines the complexity of the associated decision problem.

In the paper the authors investigate finite algebras arising from CSPs of bounded width, i.e. for which local consistency algorithms effectively decide the problem. They are able to prove that bounded width of a CSP implies that the variety generated by the associated algebra omits Hobby-McKenzie types 1 and 2. From this they can conclude the existence of CSPs that do not have bounded width. The paper concludes by giving several applications of this result by showing that various graph homomorphism problems do not have bounded width, i.e. that the corresponding graph-decision problems cannot be solved using local consistency algorithms.

title.title: Bounded width problems and algebras

editorial_contributions.text: A structure \((X,\Theta)\) on \(X\) consists of a binary reflexive relation which may be modeled as a digraph with vertices \(x\) and \(y\) in the same connected components if there exists a homomorphism from \(F\), the one-way infinite fence \((n\to m\) if \(n=m\) or \(n\) is even and \(|n-m|=1)\) whose image contains them both. The main result of this paper is Theorem 2.3: Let \((X,\Theta)\) be a finite, connected, binary reflexive structure of \(X\). If \(X\) admits a Taylor operation then it is \(n\)-connected for all \(n\geq 0\), i.e., all its (discrete) homotopy groups are trivial. Given an \(n\)-ary idempotent operation \(F\) on \(A\), an algebra, it is Taylor if \(F(X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}X,\dots,X_n)\approx F(Y_1,\dots, Y_{i-1},Y,\dots,Y_n)\) whose \(X_j,Y_j\in\{X,Y\}\) for all \(1\leq j\leq n\). In the case of intransitive structures, if \(X\) admits a Taylor operation then equivalently it is a forest and it admits a majority operation with implications for the CSP\((X)\) problem (it is in P in that case, NP-complete otherwise). Tournaments are required to be transitive instead and series-parallel structures behave in a similar manner as well in this useful addition to a growing literature of great theoretical interest.

editorial_contributions.text: The categorical product \(G\times H\) of two graphs \(G\) and \(H\) is defined by \(V(G\times H)=V(G)\times V(H)\) and \(E(G\times H)=\{[u_{1}u_{2},v_{1}v_{2}]:u_{1}v_{1}\in E(G)\) and \(u_{2}v_{2}\in E(H)\}\). For a graph \(G\), let \(G^{n}=G\times G\times \cdots \times G\) denote the \(n\)th power of \(G\). A homomorphism \(\phi \) (that is, an edge-preserving map) from the powers of \(G\) to \(G\) is called idempotent if it satisfies the identity \(\phi (x,x,\ldots ,x)=x\). \(G\) is called projective if the only if the idempotent homomorphisms from the powers of \(G\) to \(G\) are the projections, that is, the maps \(\text{pr}_{i,n}\) defined by \(\text{pr}_{i,n}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots ,x_{n})=x_{i}\). In this paper the relationship between projectivity and the structure of maximal independent sets in powers of circular graphs, Kneser graphs and truncated simplices are investigated. It is proved that all these graphs are projective.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We describe simple algebraic and combinatorial characterisations of finite relational core structures admitting finitely many obstructions. As a consequence, we show that it is decidable to determine whether a constraint satisfaction problem is first-order definable: we show the general problem to be NP-complete, and give a polynomial-time algorithm in the case of cores. A slight modification of this algorithm provides, for first-order definable CSP's, a simple poly-time algorithm to produce a solution when one exists. As an application of our algebraic characterisation of first-order CSP's, we describe a large family of L-complete CSP's.

title.title: A characterisation of first-order constraint satisfaction problems

editorial_contributions.text:
A (binary reflexive) structure is a set \(X\) equipped with a relation \(\sigma\) containing the diagonal of \(X^2\). Writing \(x\to y\) for \((x,y)\in\sigma\) we obtain an associated digraph (with loops \(x\to x\) at all vertices). \(F\) has base set \(X= \{0,1,2,\dots\}\) and \(n\to m\) provided \(n= m\) or \(n\) is even and \(|n-m|= 1\). A (weak) path in \(X\) from \(x\) to \(y\) exists iff a homomorphism \(f:F\to X\) (\(x\to y\) implies \(f(x)\to f(y)\)) has \(f(0)= x\) and \(f(n)= y\) for all \(n\geq N\). \(F^k(X,x_0)\) is the set of all homomorphisms \(f: F^k\to X\) such that for some \(N\geq 0\), \(f(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k)= x_0\) implies there is a \(\tau_i\) such that \(\tau_i= 0\) or \(\tau_i\geq N\). \(F^k(X, x_0)\) has the relation inherited from Hom\((F^k,X)\) (\(f\to g\) iff \((f(\tau)\to g(\tau))\) for \(\tau\in F^k\)) and base point \(\overline x_0\) the constant map \(f(\tau)= x_0\). Let \(\sigma_k(X, x_0)\) denote the set of path components of \(F^k(X, x_0)\) with \(|f|\) denoting the path component of \(f\). For \(f\in F^k(X, x_0)\) and \(1\leq i\leq k\) let \(N_1(f)\) denote the least nonnegative even integer \(N\) such that\(f(\tau_1,\dots, \tau_k)= x_0\) if \(\tau_i\geq N\) and \(N(f)= \max N_i(f)\). Let \(f,g\in F^k(X, x_0)\) and \(N\geq N(f)\) an even integer. Then \((f,g)_N= f(\tau_1,\dots, \tau_k)\) if \(\leq N\), \((f,g)_N= g((\tau_1)- N\), \(\tau_2,\dots, \tau_k)\) otherwise. Finally let \(|f|*|g|= |(f, g)_{N_1(f)}|\). Then it is shown that \(\sigma_k(X, x_0)= (\sigma_k(X, x_0),*,|\overline x_0|)\) is a group with identity \(|\overline x_0|\).

 With \(\sigma_k(X, x_0)\) as defined above one has a precise recipe even if somewhat complicated. Via a reductive process passing through posets and their standard realization as a simplicial complex with facets the maximal chains, it is shown that \(\sigma_{k_0}(X, x_0)\) is naturally isomorphic to the \(k\)th homotopy group of the simplicial complex of \(X\) whose simplexes are those subsets of \(X\) which are homomorphic images of finite chains. In a nice tour de force the authors provide a different way to look at these homotopy groups. As explained in the introduction, this fact can be employed to determine when the \(\sigma_k(X, x_0)\) are all trivial, and this determination plays an important role in sorting certain computational problems as being NP-complete or not.

title.title: A discrete homotopy theory for binary reflexive structures

editorial_contributions.text: The topic of interest in this paper is SysPol\((A)\), where \(A\) is a lattice, semigroup, group, ring, or module, with input: a finite sequence of ``polynomials'' \((p_i,q_j)\) of \(A\), and question: are there values \(a_i\in A\) such that \(p_j (\overline a)=q_j(\overline a)\) for all \(j\), \(\overline a=a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots\). If \(A= \langle A,F\rangle\) is a finite algebra (of finite signature) then the SysPol\((A)\) problem can be transformed to a special other problem CSP\((T)\) where it is possible to decide P or NP-complete on the basis of existence or non-existence of a compatible ``Taylor operation'' which transfers to the SysPol\((A)\) problem with the same conclusion and which can then be applied to different types of algebras, several of which are discussed in this paper. Thus, SysPol\((A)\) is in P if \(A\) is a semilattice, while SysPol\((A)\) is in NP for non-trivial lattices, for example. Or SysPol\((A)\) is in P for finite abelian groups but it is in NP for finite groups as another example. Further cases are also included in this interesting encounter of (universal) algebraic notions with a very important dichotomy of computer science yielding a plentitude of useful conclusions along the way.

title.title: Algebra and the complexity of digraph CSPs: a survey

editorial_contributions.text: This paper studies the cartesian product of graphs as an operation on classes of homomorphically equivalent graphs. The theory of graph homomorphisms is more in the spirit of coloring theory than of isomophism questions, but for some graphs (called cores) the only homomorphisms are automorphisms, and the authors use the automorphism group of a core graph to create a Cayley graph from an arbitrary graph. One of the main results of this paper is that a graph is ``hom-idempotent'' (homomorphically equivalent to its cartesian product with itself) if and only if it is homomorphically equivalent to a normal Cayley graph (``normal'' meaning that the edges are defined by a normal subset of the group). The authors also characterize ``weakly hom-idempotent'' graphs (a generalization of hom-idempotent) and include some related results and examples.

Summary: For a finite poset \(P\) let \(\text{EXT}(P)\) denote the following decision problem. Given a finite poset \(Q\) and a partial map \(f\) from \(Q\) to \(P\), decide whether \(f\) extends to a monotone total map from \(Q\) to \(P\).

 It is easy to see that \(\text{EXT}(P)\) is in the complexity class NP. In SIAM J. Comput. 28, 57--104 (1998; Zbl 0914.68075), \textit{T. Feder} and \textit{M. Y. Vardi} defined the classes of width 1 and of bounded strict width constraint satisfaction problems for finite relational structures. Both classes belong to the broader class of bounded width problems in P. We prove that for any finite poset \(P\), if \(\text{EXT}(P)\) has bounded strict width, then it has width 1. In other words, if a poset admits a near unanimity operation, it also admits a totally symmetric idempotent operation of any arity. In Fundam. Inf. 28, 165--182 (1996; Zbl 0863.68073), \textit{V. Pratt} and \textit{J. Tiuryn} proved that \(\text{SAT}(P)\), a polynomial-time equivalent of \(\text{EXT}(P)\), is NP-complete if \(P\) is a crown. We generalize Pratt and Tiuryn's result on crowns by proving that \(\text{EXT}(P)\) is NP-complete for any finite poset \(P\) which admits no nontrivial idempotent Mal'tsev condition.

editorial_contributions.text: A clone on a finite set \(A\) is a system of finitary operations on \(A\) closed under superpositions and containing all projections. For a relation \(\theta\) on \(A\), the set Pol \(\theta\) is defined to consist of all operations \(f\) on \(A\) which preserve \(\theta\). Let \(\underline{k}\) be a \(k\)-element chain with the ordering \(\leq\) and let \(M\) be the clone generated by all unary operations on \(\underline{k}\) preserving \(\leq\). The authors deal with the interval of clones \([M,\) Pol \(\leq]\). In the present paper, this interval is completely described for \(k\leq 4\). Further, the Hasse diagram for the interval in the general case is characterized. Each clone \(C\in [M,\) Pol \(\leq]\) is either depicted in the diagram or it lies in some interval \([P_h,\) Pol \(\mu_{h+1}], 3\leq h\leq k-1\), where \(P_h\) is the clone of all isotone mappings \(f\) which are either essentially unary or the image of \(f\) contains at most \(h\) elements; \(\mu_{h+1}\) is the \((h+1)\)-ary relation with \((a_1,\cdots,a_{h+1})\in \mu_{h+1}\) iff \(a_1\leq \cdots \leq a_{h+1}\) and \(|\{a_1,\cdots,a_{h+1}\}|\leq h\).

Comput. 28, No. 1, 57--104 (1998; Zbl 0914.68075)]. It has been verified for conservative problems (also known as list homomorphism problems) by \textit{A. A. Bulatov} [ACM Trans. Comput. Log. 12, No. 4, Article No. 24, 66 p. (2011; Zbl 1351.68113)]. The second author et al. [``Space complexity of list H-colouring: a dichotomy'', in: Proceedings of the Twenty-Fifth Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms, SODA 2014. Philadelphia, PA: Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM); New York, NY: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). 349--365 (2014; \url{doi:10.1137/1.9781611973402.26})] augmented this result by showing that for digraph templates H, every conservative CSP, denoted LHOM(H), is solvable in log space or is hard for NL. A conjecture of the fourth author and \textit{P. Tesson} [Theor. Comput. Sci. 410, No. 18, 1629--1647 (2009; Zbl 1172.68024)] from 2007 forecasts that when LHOM(H) is in log space, then in fact, it falls in a small subclass of log space, the set of problems expressible in symmetric Datalog. The present work verifies the conjecture for LHOM(H) (and, indeed, for the wider class of conservative CSPs with binary constraints), and by so doing sharpens the aforementioned dichotomy. A combinatorial characterization of symmetric Datalog provides the language in which the algorithmic ideas of the paper, quite different from the ones in [the first author et al., loc. cit.], are formalized.

editorial_contributions.text:
In 1990 \textit{E. Corominas} introduced projective posets and showed that every finite projective poset is strongly irreducible [C. R. Acad. Sci., Paris, Sér. I 311, 199-204 (1990; Zbl 0731.06001)]. An ordered set \(P\) is projective, if the only idempotent isotone maps from \(P^2\) to \(P\) are the two projections. A finite poset \(P\) is strongly irreducible if, whenever \(P\) is a retract of a product \(R \times Q\), where \(R\) and \(Q\) are finite, it is a retract of \(R\) or a retract of \(Q\). A poset is automorphic if it admits a fixed-point free automorphism, and minimal automorphic if it is automorphic but none of its proper retracts are. It is known that a finite ordered set has the fixed-point property if and only if it admits no minimal automorphic retract. 


Corominas conjectured that minimal automorphic posets with at least three elements are projective and therefore strongly irreducible. If this holds, then products of finite posets with the fixed-point property also possess the fixed-point property and the well-known ``product'' problem has an affirmative answer. (An affirmative answer has recently been given by M. Roddy.)


This paper investigates the connection of the product problem to the problem whether minimal automorphic posets are (strongly) irreducible or not.


Proposition. If finite irreducible posets are strongly irreducible, then the following statements are equivalent: (1) If \(P\) and \(Q\) are finite have the fixed-point property, then so does \(P \times Q\). (2) Minimal automorphic posets are irreducible.


The author also investigates the structure of minimal automorphic posets of length 2 and constructs within this class a family of projective posets. In addition he shows that sums of nontrivial ramified ordered sets over a connected poset of at least two elements are projective.

Let \(P\) be a poset. By \(\mathcal A(P)\) is denoted an algebra with the same underlying set whose term operations are all the order-preserving functions on \(P\). Let \(P\) be finite, i.e., \(P=\{x_1,\dots ,x_n\}\). We say that \(P\) dismantles to \(Q\subseteq P\) if \(Q=\{x_j,\dots ,x_n\}\) for some \(j\) and for all \(i=1,\dots ,j-1,\) \(x_i\) is an irreducible element in the subposet of \(P\) induced by \(\{x_i,\dots ,x_n\}\). A connected poset \(P\) is dismantable if it dismatles to a one-element subposet. The author proves:

Let \(P\) be a finite connected poset with at least 2 elements. Then the variety generated by \(\mathcal A(P)\) is minimal if and only if \(P\) is dismantable.

The author gives the following sufficient conditions for a graph \(K\) to be strongly projective: (1) \(K\) is a square-free, connected, ramified, non-bipartite graph. In particular \(K\) is an odd cycle. (2) \(K\) is a circular graph. In particular \(K\) is complete on at least 3 vertices. (3) \(K\) is a graph obtained from a connected, ramified, bipartite graph by adding a universal vertex. (4) \(K\) is truncated simplex. (5) \(K\) is a directly indecomposable primitive graph on at least 3 vertices. In particular, Kneser graphs are strongly projective. (6) \(K\) is a non-bipartite distance-transitive graph of diameter at least 3. 


Moreover the following equivalent conditions for a graph \(K\) with at least 3 vertices are given: (i) \(K\) is strongly projective. (ii) \(P_K\) is a projective poset. (iii) \(K\) is projective and \(I_2(K)\) consists of isolated vertices. (iv) Every pair of vertices of \(K\) admits a bipartite probe. (v) For every connected graph \(G\) with at least 2 vertices, and every \(s \geq 2\), the only maps \(f: G\times K^s \rightarrow K\) satisfying \(f(y,x,\dots,x) = x\) for all \(y\) and \(x\), are the projections \(f(y,x_1,\dots,x_s) = x_i\). 


The following definitions are used: By \(K^s\) denote the \(s\)-fold product graph \(K\times K\times \cdots \times K\); for two graphs \(K\) and \(G\) define \(K^G\) as follows: the vertices are all the functions from \(G\) to \(K\), and two such functions \(f\) and \(g\) are adjacent if they satisfy the following condition: if \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent in \(G\) then \(f(x)\) and \(g(y)\) are adjacent in \(K\). 


Let \(K\) be any graph and let \(x\geq 1\). Let \(E_s(K)\) denote the graph \(K^{K^s}\) and let \(I_s(K)\) denote the subgraph of \(E_s(K)\) consisting of the idempotent functions, i.e., those \(f\) that satisfy \(f(x,\dots,x)= x\) for all \(x\). Call a graph \(K\) strongly projective if, for every \(s \geq 2\), the only \(f\in I_x(K)\) with at least one neighbour (in \(I_s(K)\)) are projections. 


Let \(K\) be any graph. A triple \((P;Q,q)\) is a \(K\)-coloured graph if \(P\) is a graph, \(Q\) is a (possibly empty) set of vertices of \(P\) and \(q\) is a function with domain \(Q\) and codomain \(K\). Let \(\theta\) be a \(K\)-ary relation on \(K\), \(k\geq 1\). A quadruple \((P,Q,q,R)\) is a \(K\)-probe for \(\theta\) (or \(\theta\) admits the probe \((P,Q,q,R)\)) if (i) \((P,Q,q)\) is a \(K\)-coloured graph and (ii) \(R = (v_1, \dots,v_k)\) is a \(k\)-tuple of vertices of \(P\) such that 
\[
 \theta = \{(f(v_1),\dots,f(v_k)): f \text{ is a map from } P \text{ to } K \text{ that extends }q\}. 
\]
 


Let \(K\) be a graph. If \(a\) is a vertex of \(K\) let \(N_a\) denote its neighbourhood in \(K\); i.e., the set of all vertices of \(K\) adjacent to \(a\). We say that a graph is ramified if for all vertices \(a\) and \(b\) of \(K\) we have that \(N_a \subseteq N_b\) implies \(a = b\). If \(K\) is a ramified, connected, non-bipartite graph, the neighbourhood poset of \(K\) is the poset \(P = \mathcal{P}_K\) of all non-empty intersections of neighbourhoods of \(K\) ordered by inclusion. A poset is projective if the only idempotent order-preserving operations on \(P\) are projections. 


We say that a graph is square-free if it contains no (not necessarily induced) 4-cycle. \(K\) is a truncated simplex. 


Let \(r,l\) be positive integers such that \(r < l/2\). The circular graph \(\text{Circ}(r,l)\) is defined as follows: 
\[
 \begin{aligned} V(\text{Circ}(r,l)) & = \{0,1,\dots,l-1\},\\ E(\text{Circ}(r,l)) & = \{[i,j]: i-j \in \{r,r+1,\dots, l-r\}\}. \end{aligned} 
\]
 The truncated \(n\)-simplex \(T_n\) is defined as follows: 
\[
 \begin{aligned} V(T_n) & = \{(i,j) \in \{ 0,1,\dots,n-1\}^2: i\not= j\},\\ E(T_n) & = \{[(i,j),(k,l)]: i = k,\;j\not= l \text{ or } i=l,\;j=k\}. \end{aligned} 
\]
 A vertex in a graph \(K\) is universal if it is adjacent to all other vertices.

editorial_contributions.text: The authors prove an analog of a lemma by Mal'tsev and deduce the following analog of a result of Rosenberg: Let \(Q\) is a finite poset with \(n\) elements, \(k\) denotes the \(k\)-element chain and \(h\) is an integer such that \({2 \leq h < n \leq k}\). Consider the set of all order-preserving maps from \(Q\) to \(\underline{k}\) whose image contains at most \(h\) elements, viewed as an \(n\)-ary relation \(\mu_{Q, h}\) on \(\underline{k}\). Then an \(l\)-ary order-preserving operation \(f\) on \(\underline{k}\) preserves this relation if and only if it is either (i) essentially unary or (ii) the cardinality of \(f(e(Q))\) is at most \(h\) for every isotone map \(e: Q \rightarrow \underline{k}^l\).

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(L\) be a lattice and let \(\mathbb{R}\) denote the set of real numbers. A function \(f: L\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is called supermodular if it satisfies \(f(x)+f(y)\leq f(x\wedge y)+f(x\vee y)\) for all \(x, y\in L.\) Note that supermodular functions play an important role in some applications, such as in mathematical economics, operations research or computer science. In the last domain, supermodular functions occur in the study of the complexity of certain optimisation problems called maximum constraint satisfaction problems. We need one more concept: Let \(K\) be a sublattice of \(L.\) \(K\) is said to be supermodular (in \(L\)) if, for any \(x\in K\) and \(y\in L\), at least one of the elements \(x\wedge y, x\vee y\) belongs to \(K.\) It is easy to verify that an ideal or a filter or a union of an ideal and a filter is a supermodular sublattice of \(L.\) The following result is also easy to derive: Let \(f\) be a 0-1 valued function on \(L\). Then \(f\) is supermodular on \(L\) iff \(\{x\in L: f(x)=1\}\) is a supermodular sublattice of \(L\).

The main result describes the supermodular sublattices of a finite lattice \(L,\) where \(L\) is a direct product of non-trivial relatively complemented lattices.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: The Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) and its counting counterpart appears under different guises in many areas of mathematics, computer science, statistical physics, and elsewhere. Its structural and algorithmic properties have demonstrated to play a crucial role in many of those applications. For instance, topological properties of the solution set such as connectedness is related to the hardness of CSPs over random structures. In approximate counting and statistical physics, where CSPs emerge in the form of spin systems, mixing properties and the uniqueness of Gibbs measures have been heavily exploited for approximating partition functions or the free energy of spin systems. Additionally, in the decision CSPs, structural properties of the relational structures involved -- like, for example, dismantlability -- and their logical characterizations have been instrumental for determining the complexity and other properties of the problem. 

In spite of the great diversity of those features, there are some eerie similarities between them. These were observed and made more precise in the case of graph homomorphisms by \textit{G. R. Brightwell} and \textit{P. Winkler} [J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 78, No. 1, 141--166 (2000; Zbl 1030.05101)], who showed that the structural property of dismantlability of the target graph, the connectedness of the set of homomorphisms, good mixing properties of the corresponding spin system, and the uniqueness of Gibbs measure are all equivalent. In this paper we go a step further and demonstrate similar connections for arbitrary CSPs. This requires much deeper understanding of dismantling and the structure of the solution space in the case of relational structures, and new refined concepts of mixing introduced by the first author [Ergodic Theory Dyn. Syst. 38, No. 5, 1658--1696 (2016; Zbl 1398.37021)]. In addition, we develop properties related to the study of valid extensions of a given partially defined homomorphism, an approach that turns out to be novel even in the graph case. We also add to the mix the combinatorial property of finite duality and its logic counterpart, FO-definability, studied by \textit{B. Larose} et al. [Log. Methods Comput. Sci. 3, No. 4, Paper 6, 22 p. (2007; Zbl 1131.68098)].

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1414.68003].

editorial_contributions.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set, \(\text{Card }A\geq 3\). Recall that each clone on \(A\) is isomorphic to a clone \(\text{Pol }R\), where \(R\) is a set of finitary relations on \(A\) and \(\text{Pol }R\) is the set of all the finitary operations on \(A\) that preserves all the relations in \(R\). title.title: Sous-clones maximaux du clone des opérations monotones sur un ordre borné fini. (Maximal subclones of the clone of isotone operations on a bounded finite order)

editorial_contributions.text: \textit{D. Greenwell} and \textit{L. Lovász} [Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hung. 25, 335-340 (1974; Zbl 0294.05108)] showed that, if a graph \(G\) is not \(n\)-colourable, then the product \(G\times K_{n}\) is uniquely \(n\)-colourable. This result is extended to higher powers. In fact, the following more general result is proved: If a connected graph \(G\) does not admit a homomorphism into \(K\), where \(K\) is an odd cycle or a complete graph of order at least 3, then, for every \(s\geq 1,\) the graph \(G\times K^{s}\) admits exactly \(s\) homomorphisms into \(K\) (up to automorphisms of \(K\)). The proof relies on results concerning exponential graphs and strongly projective graphs. Given two graphs, \(G\) and \(K\), the exponential graph \(K^{G}\) has as its vertices all the functions from \(G\) to \(K\) and two such functions \(f\) and \(g\) are adjacent if they satisfy the following condition: if \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent in \(G\) then \(f\left( x\right) \) and \(f\left( y\right) \) are adjacent in \(K.\) The graph \(G^{G^{s}}\) is denoted by \(E_{s}(G).\) A graph \(G\) is called strongly projective if, for every \(s\geq 2\), the only idempotent functions in \(E_{s}(G)\) with at least one neighbour are the projections. First, strongly projective graphs are characterized in terms of their neighbourhood poset and then a detailed description of the graphs \(E_{s}(K)\) is given for the case where \(s\geq 2\) and \(K\) is an odd cycle or a \(K_{n};\) \(n\geq 3\).

title.title: A completeness criterion for isotone operations on a finite chain

editorial_contributions.text: The authors generalize some known results to arbitrary finite posets. They show that for every finite poset the existence of Gumm or Jónsson operations is equivalent to the existence of a near unanimity function in the clone of isotone operations. Finite connected posets satisfying these equivalent conditions are characterized by the property that their idempotent subalgebras are dismantlable. They obtain that the problem of determining if a finite poset admits a near unanimity function is decidable.

editorial_contributions.text:
This very dense and high-level article aims at completely classifying the computational complexity of the list H-colouring problem, a rather famous graph problem.

A certain number of pre-requisites, at different levels, are necessary for the reader to be able to understand the contents of the paper: graphs, graph colouring, graph homomorphism; complexity classes (beyond the usual NP-completeness), such as NL- or L-completeness; first-order logic; constraint satisfaction problems. Some other advanced notions and terms are also needed to be known -- the paper is not self-contained in that sense.

Altogether, this paper is not for the faint-hearted.

That said, the paper, although very dense in terms of results, is clearly written, and its somewhat complicated structure is very clearly described in its first few pages. More importantly, its results cover a wide spectrum, and altogether lead to a strong paper.

editorial_contributions.text: Let \(Q\) be a poset and \(P\) be its subposet. A monotone mapping \(h\) from \(Q\) to \(P\) is called a retraction from \(Q\) onto \(P\) if \(h(x)=x\) for every \(x\in P\). The poset retraction problem for a poset \(P\) is whether a given poset \(Q\) containing \(P\) as a subposet admits a retraction onto \(P\). In the paper, this problem is investigated for series-parallel posets \(P\), i.e., for posets \(P\) which are constructed from singletons by means of disjoint unions and ordinal sums. The authors describe posets which admit a retraction onto \(P\) for \(P\) from a certain class of finite series-parallel posets.

title.title: Retractions onto series-parallel posets

editorial_contributions.text: If \(P\) is a partially ordered set, then its subsets are called the coalitions of \(P\). For every coalitions \(X\) and \(Y\) of \(P\), \(X\leq Y\) means that there exists an injection \(\varphi:X\to Y\) such that \(x\leq \varphi(x)\) for each \(x\in X\). Then the set \({\mathcal L}(P)\) of all coalitions of \(P\) equipped with \(\leq\) is a partially ordered set. If \({\mathcal L}(P)\) is a lattice then \({\mathcal L}(P)\) is called the coalition lattice of \(P\). (Note that this concept has roots in game theory.) In the paper it is shown that every coalition lattice \({\mathcal L}(P)\) satisfies the Jordan-Hölder chain condition and that \({\mathcal L}(P)\) determines \(P\) up to isomorphism. Furthermore, a coalition \(X\) is said to be winning if \(P\setminus X\leq X\). The winning coalitions of a coalition lattice are shown to form a dual ideal in \({\mathcal L}(P)\).

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Let \(A\) be a finite set, \(|A|\geq 2\), let \(C\) be a clone on \(A\) and \(r\) a unary member of \(C\) satisfying \(r^2=r\). We investigate the relationship between the lattice of clones containing \(C\) and the lattice of clones on \(R=r(A)\). We obtain a criterion to determine if the function \(r\) is invertible in \(C\) by inspecting the relations preserved by all members of \(C\). We give conditions on the operation \(r\) to insure that a given clone \(D\) covers \(C\) in the lattice of clones on \(A\).

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: The \textsc{Surjective \texttt{H}-Colouring} problem is to test if a given graph allows a vertex-surjective homomorphism to a fixed graph \texttt{H}. The complexity of this problem has been well studied for undirected (partially) reflexive graphs. We introduce endo-triviality, the property of a structure that all of its endomorphisms that do not have range of size 1 are automorphisms, as a means to obtain complexity-theoretic classifications of \textsc{Surjective \texttt{H}-Colouring} in the case of reflexive digraphs. \textit{H. Chen} [Algebra Univers. 72, No. 4, 393--401 (2014; Zbl 1308.08001)] proved, in the setting of constraint satisfaction problems, that \textsc{Surjective \texttt{H}-Colouring} is \textsf{NP}-complete if \texttt{H} has the property that all of its polymorphisms are essentially unary. We give the first concrete application of his result by showing that every endo-trivial reflexive digraph \texttt{H} has this property. We then use the concept of endo-triviality to prove, as our main result, a dichotomy for \textsc{Surjective \texttt{H}-Colouring} when \texttt{H} is a reflexive tournament: if \texttt{H} is transitive, then \textsc{Surjective \texttt{H}-Colouring} is in \textsf{NL}, otherwise it is \textsf{NP}-complete. By combining this result with some known and new results we obtain a complexity classification for \textsc{Surjective \texttt{H}-Colouring} when \texttt{H} is a partially reflexive digraph of size at most 3.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1381.68010].

Summary: We completely classify the computational complexity of the list \(H\)-colouring problem for graphs (with possible loops) in combinatorial and algebraic terms: for every graph \(H\) the problem is either NP-complete, NL-complete, L-complete or is first-order definable; descriptive complexity equivalents are given as well via Datalog and its fragments. Our algebraic characterisations match important conjectures in the study of constraint satisfaction problems.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: We give a complexity dichotomy for the Quantified Constraint Satisfaction Problem QCSP(H) when \(H\) is a reflexive tournament. It is well-known that reflexive tournaments can be split into a sequence of strongly connected components \(H_1,\dots,H_n\) so that there exists an edge from every vertex of \(H_i\) to every vertex of \(H_j\) if and only if \(i<j\). We prove that if \(H\) has both its initial and final strongly connected component (possibly equal) of size \(1\), then QCSP\((H)\) is in NL and otherwise QCSP\((H)\) is NP-hard.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1473.68018].
